## Overview

The Baure people are an ethnic group living in the Beni Department of Bolivia. The 2012 census recorded 3,328 people, of whom 58 spoke Baure natively. The Baure language is an endangered Arawakan language of northwest Bolivia and belongs more specifically to the Southern Arawakan branch, which also includes the Moxo languages. Baure-speaking communities are associated with the Baure municipality and surrounding communities such as El Carmen. The language and people’s history are described in relation to the Llanos de Mojos region, whose history is divided into the pre-Hispanic era, the era of the Jesuits, the late-19th-century rubber-exploitation period, mid-20th-century reforms, and indigenous awareness beginning in the 1990s.

## Material culture

### Architecture

 The Baure language source mentions *wer* “house” as an example of a possession noun, but gives no architectural description.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 The Baure language source gives *yakis* “firewood” and *jopi* “pitcher” as linguistic examples.

## Music & performance

Baure is used in songs and ritual conversations. The language source specifically identifies the Song of the Baures, which is sung as part of festivals. It also states that Baure is spoken in limited contexts including greetings, jokes, folktales, ritual conversations, and songs.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources mention festivals only as a context for singing the Song of the Baures. The language source also identifies ritual conversations as one of the limited contexts in which Baure is spoken.

## Oral tradition & literature

Baure is used in folktales, jokes, greetings, ritual conversations, and songs. Some Bible portions have been translated into Bauré. The language source states that literacy workshops in the low counties and study of the language have contributed to increased use, with many speakers beginning to use Baure daily and transmit it to their children.

## Language & religion

Baure or Bauré is a severely endangered Arawakan language spoken in the Beni Department of Bolivia. The source describes it as part of the Southern Arawakan languages and says it is most closely related in lexical and grammatical terms to the Trinitarian and Ignatian Moxo languages. Three dialects or languages are recognized as part of Baure: Baure proper, Carmelito, and Joaquiniano. Carmelito was spoken by only one person in 2016, while the last fluent speaker of Joaquiniano, Concepción Mercado Bayo, nicknamed Mama Concha, died in 2005. In 2010, around 20 native speakers remained according to the evidence available; another account gives 40 speakers. Since Supreme Decree N.25894 in 2000, Baure has been considered one of Bolivia’s official indigenous languages, a status included in the Political Constitution passed on 7 February 2009.
